title: Ad-Duha: the orphan and the asker
hookLine: did He not find you an orphan and shelter you, so don't be harsh with orphans or turn askers away (93:6–10)

lines: I REMEMBER WHAT IT WAS LIKE.
cards: Ask someone who grew up without much why they notice certain people, and the answer is often short: I remember what it was like. The one who went to school hungry notices the kid with no lunch.
The one who was new in the country notices the family that doesn't speak the language yet. Memory turns into attention.
The second half of Surah ad-Duha asks the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ to remember where he came from, and then tells him what to do with the memory.

teach.b: The surah asks three questions, in Pickthall's translation: Did He not find thee an orphan and protect thee? Did He not find thee wandering and direct thee? Did He not find thee destitute and enrich thee?
The early biographies fill in each line. His father died before he was born. His mother, they say, died when he was about six, and his grandfather, who took him in, two years later.
Then his uncle Abu Talib raised him. An orphan three times over, and each time, someone sheltered him.

Wandering, commentators say, means searching, not yet guided, before revelation came. Destitute: he was poor, and commentators often connect his later means to his marriage to Khadijah and his work in trade.
Then the surah turns those memories into two instructions: Therefor the orphan oppress not, Therefor the beggar drive not away.
The Arabic for the beggar is as-sa'il, the one who asks. Some commentators read it as covering both: the one who asks for money or food, and the one who asks a question, who comes to learn.
Don't brush off either one, or sigh at them, or make them feel small for asking.
The Prophet said, in a hadith in Bukhari, holding up two fingers side by side: I and the one who cares for an orphan will be in Paradise like this.
You were sheltered, so shelter. You were guided, so answer the one who asks.

how: Care for orphans holds a special place in Muslim practice, from sponsoring orphans to supporting orphanages, and many Muslims recall 93:9–10 when someone asks them for help or a question.

o: the charity handed to orphans at the festival
the bright morning, a surah of comfort and care
the hour of night when revelation came down

games.q: what's inside the surah — tap the pairs.
p: the one who asks, for help or to learn
the orphan's carer and the Prophet

s: the Prophet lost his father before he was born
the biographies say his mother died when he was about six, his grandfather two years later.
as-sa'il means only a beggar asking for money
it's the one who asks: for help, or with a question.
the surah asks the Prophet to forget where he came from
it asks him to remember, and turn the memory into kindness.

games.q: you were once an orphan, and someone took you in. now an orphan and a stranger with a question come to your door. what does the surah say?
o: help whoever you have time for
don't be harsh with the orphan, and don't drive the asker away
games.why: therefor the orphan oppress not, therefor the beggar drive not away (93:9–10). you were sheltered, so shelter.

practice: Remember one time you needed something and someone gave it: a meal, a ride, an answer, a place to stay. Picture their face, and let the memory of being helped come back.
Then decide how you'll meet the next person who asks: a yes if you can, a kind answer if you can't, and no sigh.

wordCard.voice: Ad-Duha. The bright morning, and the surah that says: you were an orphan and were sheltered, so don't turn the asker away. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the one who asks, whether for help or to learn; from 93:10.

carryVoice: Your line: don't turn the asker away. The memory of need is meant to become kindness. One hundred eighty-seven days now.

sources.q: Did He not find thee an orphan and protect (thee)? Did He not find thee wandering and direct (thee)? Did He not find thee destitute and enrich (thee)? Therefor the orphan oppress not, Therefor the beggar drive not away,
